segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another verb that contracts in this way, losing its last 'e', like poder becoming podría, is haber, to have.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I would have", how would it be? You're going to add the -ía on haber, and it's going to lose its 'e' like poder did. So how would it sound?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habría. So, habría means I would have, you would have (formally), he would have, she would have, it would have. Which means now you can make sentences like "I would have gone", "I would have eaten something, but..." etcetera. So let's practice with this. How would you say "I would have gone"? What's "to go" first?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ir. How would you make "gone" from "to go"? What is the rule to get "gone" from "to go"? The version that we need after haber, after any version of haber, it doesn't matter if it's he, hemos or habría. It's the version of the verb that comes after haber. How do we get that version?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Okay, I take away -ir, the ending. It's the whole verb, but whatever, it doesn't matter. I'm taking away the ending -ir and I'm putting -ido. Good. "I would have gone"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Habría ido. "We would have eaten", how would that be? "We would have eaten".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Habríamos comido. We could even make a sentence now like, "We would have been able to go". "We would have been able to go". And as long as you tackle each individual part individually, you will stay in control and you will be able to make these apparently really complicated sentences, which are actually quite simple because they take the same structure in English and Spanish. So, "we would have", how would that be, "we would have"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Been able", so what's "to be able", related to power?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Aha. Poder is "to be able". How would you make that "been able", or just the version after haber? What does it do when it comes after haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Habríamos podido ir. "We would have been able to go". Good. You could say "They would have been able to eat", so divide it up block by block and it's very simple. "They would have"...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habrían podido comer. So if you were to say something like "They would have come to eat", then "come" is a verb of motion. So how would you say "They would have come to eat"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habrían venido a comer, because we have venir, a verb of motion connecting to another "to" form. Good. With this very useful structure of habría, habrían, habríamos, "would have", you could also say something like "I would have liked it". You just need to think in this Spanglish, in this in-between language, the literal translation of how we want to say it in English and then convert it. So, "I would have liked it" is "It would have pleased me". "It would have pleased me". So to not lose our control and to stay in control of this process, where is the first place we want our thoughts to go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, "it would have". Good. So what is "it would have"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Pleased", so it's gustar after haber. So maybe it's better to think of it in this way: I'm finding the version of the verb after haber, instead of actually trying to find the translation of the word, because the versions after "have" are so different in English. We have eaten, gone, walked. So if we are looking for walked, gone, or eaten, and we forget that it's just the version after haber, we might be looking for a very long time, huh? So, the version after haber, we have -ado or -ido, no?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So now we can make the sentence, "It would have pleased me", "I would have liked it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me habría gustado. Good. So "I would have liked it". How would you say "We would have liked it"? So "It would have pleased us".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Nos habría gustado. And maybe you might want to say "We would have liked them". First give me the Spanglish, the literal translation in English. So we want to say "We would have liked them". What is the literal translation of how we put it into Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perfect. Well done. "They would have pleased us". So now you are, you have all you need to make that sentence.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos habrían gustado. "They would have pleased us", "We would have liked them". So we just saw some complicated structures with this "would", which is especially useful because we can make "could" and we can make "would have". We can also make "should" with this "would". What was "to owe" or "must", which was related to "debt" in English?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Deber. Good, -er verb, deber. Now if you say "would owe", this means "should". How would you say then "I should, he should, it should, she should, you (formal) should"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Debería. Good. How would you say "You should come to my house"? "You should come to my house", informal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberías venir a mi casa. Good. "You should come to my house to eat". "You should come to my house to eat", informally still.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Deberías venir a mi casa a comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberías venir a comer a mi casa or deberías venir a mi casa a comer, both are perfectly fine. Well done. How would you say "we should"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "we should speak"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Here, "speak" is "to speak". The confusion might come that in English after "can", after "should", after "must", we don't say "to". "I must eat", not "I must to eat". "I can eat", not "I can to eat". In Spanish, you're just using the "to" form afterwards. So, "we should speak", "we should speak".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "We should speak", deberíamos hablar. "We should speak about it", and we said we don't need "about".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberíamos hablarlo. "We should speak about it", "we should speak it". What if you wanted to say "we should speak to him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberíamos hablarle. This could actually be to him or to her or to you, formal, no? Deberíamos hablarle. What if you wanted to say "we should speak to them" or "we should speak to you guys"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberíamos hablarles. How would you say "we should speak with him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So choosing these structures, you get around the ambiguity of deberíamos hablarle, which could mean him or her or you formal. And if we use con, we see very clearly who we mean: deberíamos hablar con él, deberíamos hablar con ella. Good. "To give" is dar. Dar, "to give". How would you say "I would give"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "They would give me" or "to me"?
